item.title: The BRUIT-FM "open data" noise reduction challenge
item.description: arXiv:2606.05941v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The BRUIT-FM Challenge asks participants to reduce ''noise'' --- defined as any signal that masks the signal of interest --- on an open dataset of real and synthetic broadband seafloor seismology data. The dataset includes signals from earthquakes, ocean infragravity waves and seafloor currents. It also includes training datasets of synthetic data with reference solutions. Participants are asked to remove or separate these signals to obtain the best earthquake and seafloor compliance signals. The authors will make a first assessment of the submissions, based on noise reduction, signal deformation and ease of use. Participants are invited to a community workshop, in which they will validate the preliminary assessment and collaborate on a community paper describing the results, identifying promising pathways and proposing new directions. The best results will be added to a new version of the dataset, which will persist as a benchmark for future developments.
item.dc:creator: Wayne C Crawford (IPGP-UAR / UAR3454, IPGP - UMR\_7154, LIENSs, ULR), Stephan Ker (GEO-OCEAN), Simon Rebeyrol (GEO-OCEAN), Laurent Duval (IFPEN)

item.title: Data-driven reconstruction of spatiotemporal phase dynamics for traveling and oscillating patterns via Bayesian inference
item.description: arXiv:2604.23727v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Building on the phase reduction theory formulated for reaction-diffusion systems with spatial translational symmetry, we develop a data-driven method that reconstructs the spatiotemporal phase dynamics of traveling and oscillating patterns. Spatiotemporal phase dynamics are described by spatial and temporal phases that represent the position and oscillation of the pattern, respectively. Using Bayesian inference, our method directly reconstructs phase equations from time-series data. When tested on simulation data from coupled Gray-Scott models exhibiting traveling breathers, the method accurately reconstructs the deterministic part of the phase equations in the weak-noise regime, in which the phase dynamics converge to a linearly stable fixed point.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Arai, Toshio Aoyagi, Yoji Kawamura

item.title: Hyperstatistics
item.description: arXiv:2604.24783v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a general approach, named by us hyperstatistics, to treat complex systems, in which Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics breaks down at the domain level of the system. Hyperstatistics preserves the concavity of the nonadditive $q$-entropy. We obtain analytical closed-form expressions for the here proposed ($q, n$)-generalized Boltzmann factor $B_q^{n}$ considering uniform, $\gamma$, Log-normal, F, and the $q$-$\gamma$ probability distribution functions. Remarkably, for all investigated distribution functions, $B_q^{n}$ reduces to a $q$-exponential-type function. To demonstrate the applicability of hyperstatistics, we use a table top experiment of the discharge of a capacitor considering $\gamma$-distributed relaxation times, the pressure decay over time associated with the pumping of $^4$He lines of a closed cycle cryostat, midrapidity data for $\textit{p}$-Pb collisions at the LHC, as well as data set for acceleration distribution in turbulent systems. Furthermore, we deduce the power-law-like $\textit{universal}$ dielectric response using a $q$-generalized $\gamma$-distribution function proposed in this work. Hyperstatistics is applicable to systems with inherent non-Boltzmann-Gibbsian statistics at the domain level. We demonstrate that at the domain level hyperstatistics and superstatistics are equivalent, while at the macroscopic level hyperstatistics recovers superstatistics for $q \to 1$ because the Boltzmann-Gibbs character of the domains is restored, as well as Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics for $n \to \infty$.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Squillante, Samuel M. Soares, Constantino Tsallis, Mariano de Souza

item.title: Intrinsic instantaneous coarse-to-fine recoverability in multiscale chaos: The Lorenz-96 system
item.description: arXiv:2607.08323v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In multiscale chaotic systems, a central question for closure is how much of an unresolved fine-scale target can be inferred from a simultaneous coarse observation. For a specified observation-target pair, we quantify instantaneous recoverability under the invariant snapshot measure as the fraction of target variance explained by conditioning on the retained coarse variables. Evaluating this quantity across scales produces a scale-resolved recoverability map. Applied to the Lorenz-96 system across a range of forcings, the maps reveal a strongly nonuniform landscape: lower-wavenumber targets have little variance explained by the retained lower modes, while a finite band of higher modes exhibits partial recoverability once the retained scales reach the energetically active intermediate range. Recoverability onset is organized around a reference cutoff at which two retained modes can directly couple to the target through the quadratic nonlinearity, although its precise location depends on attractor statistics. Across the tested forcings, this qualitative onset structure persists while recoverability decreases, leaving a larger fraction of target variance unexplained in more strongly driven regimes. This definition identifies the maximal explained-variance fraction attainable by instantaneous deterministic models under squared loss; the estimated maps provide a scale-dependent diagnostic for closure modeling.
item.dc:creator: Zhongfeng Xu, Junfeng Chen

item.title: Anomaly detection for multijet scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2609.00132v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Signals of physics beyond the Standard Model continue to resist discovery at the LHC. Recent years have seen the proliferation of new anomaly detection techniques, promising discovery with significantly fewer model assumptions than traditional approaches. Strategies based on weak supervision have been especially successful, but so far were largely limited in scope by their reliance on a resonance manifesting a decay into a pair of jets. In this work, we demonstrate that a well-established idea from jet substructure physics - recursive soft drop - in combination with the CATHODE technique for anomaly detection can be used to simultaneously perform anomaly detection for signals with an arbitrary number of jets in the final state, greatly increasing the scope of such searches.
item.dc:creator: Gregor Kasieczka, Sung Hak Lim, Louis Moureaux, Tore von Schwartz, David Shih, Chitrakshee Yede
